question: According to Girls Who Code, how long did it take in years for the percentage of computer scientists that were women to change by 13% from a starting point of 37%?

history.name: user
history.content: According to Girls Who Code, how long did it take in years for the percentage of computer scientists that were women to change by 13% from a starting point of 37%?

history.name: Orchestrator
history.content: Task: Determine, per Girls Who Code (GWC), the number of years it took for a 13% change from a starting point of 37% women among computer scientists. We will rely on GWC's own language and any official pages/reports. Team: Assistant (analysis), WebSurfer (web lookups), FileSurfer (local files if any). Plan: 1) Find the precise GWC wording and any years attached. 2) If GWC uses contextual phrases like “today,” identify the implied year via annual reports/archives. 3) Compute the duration in years. WebSurfer, please locate a GWC page or report that mentions 37% and 24% with context.

history.name: Orchestrator
history.content: WebSurfer: search site:girlswhocode.com for '37% 24% computer scientists today 1995 Girls Who Code'. Extract exact phrasing and whether any specific years are given.

history.name: WebSurfer
history.content: Search results show Girls Who Code 'About Us' page prominently. The snippet reads: 'In 1995, 37% of computer scientists were women. Today, it’s only 24%.' No explicit year is attached to 'today' in the snippet. I can open the page to confirm the exact wording and surrounding context.

history.name: Orchestrator
history.content: Open the GWC About Us page and quote the exact language around the 37% and 24% figures. Also check if any nearby section or footer indicates the page’s last updated year.

history.name: WebSurfer
history.content: On Girls Who Code | About Us: The text states, 'The gender gap in computing is getting worse. In 1995, 37% of computer scientists were women. Today, it’s only 24%.' The page itself displays current program stats (e.g., students served) consistent with 2024 updates, but this particular sentence does not specify the endpoint year for 'today.' No explicit date is attached to the 24% line; the page metadata shows it has been modified in recent years. Conclusion: GWC About Us confirms 1995 at 37% and 'today' at 24%, but does not state the exact year for 'today.'

history.name: Orchestrator
history.content: Because GWC uses 'today' without a year on About Us, let’s triangulate via GWC research or co-branded reports that discuss the historical peak (often cited as 37% in the mid-1980s for degrees). WebSurfer, look for a GWC research page or a report (e.g., Accenture x GWC) that mentions 37% historically and offers timelines hitting 24%.

history.name: WebSurfer
history.content: Found: Accenture & Girls Who Code report 'Cracking the Gender Code' (2016) which references historical participation trends; external sources often note the peak near 37% around 1984 for CS degrees. Separately, GWC’s About Us page uses 'computer scientists' and states 'In 1995, 37%... today 24%.' These are subtly different metrics (degrees vs workforce/profession), but both align around a 13-point change to 24% in recent decades. No single GWC page I see right now assigns a specific year to the 24% in the About Us phrasing.

history.name: Assistant
history.content: Synthesis so far: Two common reference points within or adjacent to GWC materials: 1) Peak or starting point near 37% in 1984 (often degrees) and 2) 'In 1995, 37% of computer scientists were women. Today, it’s 24%.' If we interpret a 13-point change to 24% occurring circa mid-2000s (some timelines show low/mid 2000s settling around mid-20s), one plausible duration from 1984 to around 2006 would be about 22 years. That would directly match a 13-point drop from 37% to 24% across roughly two decades. This looks like a strong candidate interval. We could answer 22 years based on that interpretation.

history.name: Orchestrator
history.content: Let’s not finalize yet. We should validate what GWC likely means by 'today' for the 24% figure on their About page. WebSurfer, search for Girls Who Code press releases or annual reports where the '24%' is explicitly present and tied to a specific 'current' year (e.g., 2017, 2018, 2019). If we can identify the earliest year they used 24% as 'today,' we can compute a duration from 1995 accordingly.

history.name: WebSurfer
history.content: Looking at external traces and archives: Mentions of 'today 24%' appear in GWC public-facing materials in the late 2010s. Some third-party references attribute 'women hold 24–26% of computing jobs' to 2017–2019 years. I find references to GWC using the 24% line in materials around 2018. While I don’t see a single GWC page explicitly stating '24% (as of 2018),' it appears consistent that by 2018, GWC was citing 'today' at 24%.

history.name: Orchestrator
history.content: Given that About Us explicitly says 'In 1995, 37%… Today, 24%,' and evidence suggests 'today' was in use by 2018, using 1995 as the start and 2018 as the endpoint yields a duration of 23 years. Even though we earlier considered a 22-year estimate from the 1984 framing, GWC’s own About page anchors the 37% specifically to 1995. Therefore, I will update the duration to 23 years.

history.name: Assistant
history.content: Answer: 23 years. This follows the Girls Who Code About Us framing (1995 at 37%, 'today' ≈ 2018 at 24%), producing a 13-point change over 23 years. If needed, we can further corroborate the first appearance of the '24%' phrasing in GWC’s archives.

history.name: Orchestrator
history.content: Let’s continue validating. WebSurfer, check the Internet Archive for Girls Who Code’s About Us page snapshots in 2016–2019 to see when the 'today, it’s only 24%' phrasing appears, and whether 2018 is indeed the earliest consistent use.

history.name: WebSurfer
history.content: Archive snapshots indicate that earlier versions sometimes cited '26%' for computing occupations (varies by snapshot), and later iterations coalesced around '24%.' By 2018–2019, '24%' is visible on public-facing pages. This supports the interpretation that 'today' could map to 2018 or shortly thereafter.

history.name: Orchestrator
history.content: We’ll keep 23 years as the working duration given the About Us anchor (1995→~2018). If more precise archival evidence is found, we can adjust, but for now we maintain 23. Next steps (optional): verify any GWC media kits or partner reports from 2018 citing 24% explicitly to pin the exact month. Continuing monitoring for any updated phrasing.
